findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the fsutil.py citations to :103 (tempfile.mkstemp) and :119 (os.replace).
evidence: Plan: "`tempfile.mkstemp` in the same directory plus `os.replace` (`src/rebar/_store/fsutil.py:102` and `:118`)"
fsutil.py:103: `fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=directory, prefix=f".{base}.", suffix=".tmp")`
fsutil.py:119: `os.replace(tmp, path)  # atomic on the same filesystem`
findings.finding: The plan cites `src/rebar/_store/fsutil.py:102` and `:118` for tempfile.mkstemp and os.replace. In the source, mkstemp is at line 103 and os.replace at line 119. Lines 102 and 118 are `base = os.path.basename(path)` and `os.chmod(tmp, ...)`. The claim itself (same-directory temp file, then replace, so a new inode) is correct; only the line references are off by one.
scenarios: A reviewer or implementer who follows the citations lands on basename/chmod, not on the calls that justify the inode oracle.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record on the ticket two red runs of the NEW oracles. (a) With atomic_write stubbed to a no-op on the post-deletion call, test_cache_invalidated_on_file_deletion fails. (b) With an extra forced rewrite during the hit step, test_cache_miss_on_same_size_inplace_rewrite fails.
evidence: "Failure path: with the coarse-mtime fixture applied and the old mtime assertion kept, test_cache_invalidated_on_file_deletion fails"
No red step exercises the new oracles against a cache that skips or adds a rewrite
Root cause notes the line-372 hit oracle "cannot detect a regression there", yet no check shows the replacement can
findings.finding: The failure path shows only that the OLD mtime oracle fails under the coarse-mtime fixture. That validates the fixture, but not the new oracles. No step shows that the new inode/dir_hash/state assertions fail when the cache misbehaves: the deletion test when the post-deletion rewrite is suppressed, or the in-place test's hit check when a spurious rewrite happens. Green new oracles alone cannot tell 'detects the regression' apart from 'vacuously passes'.
scenarios: The new hit check is written against the wrong path or the wrong stat field and passes whether or not the cache is rewritten
The deletion test's dir_hash comparison reads the same envelope twice and passes trivially
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Testing bullet: 'Oracle sensitivity: under the fixture, temporarily (i) make the wrapper skip the second write and confirm the deletion test fails on the inode/dir_hash assertion; (ii) make the wrapper re-invoke the real atomic_write during the hit step and confirm the in-place test's hit assertion fails. Record both outputs on the ticket.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a failure-path demonstration for the in-place-rewrite HIT oracle: force a cache rewrite where a HIT is expected and show that the inode-unchanged assertion fails while the old mtime assertion passes. Correct the Approach claim that the old oracle fails deterministically for both tests.
evidence: "Every run then executes both tests under the conditions of the failing host. The old mtime oracle fails deterministically there, and the new oracles must pass."
"On a coarse-timestamp host that check passes even when the cache was rewritten, so it cannot detect a regression there."
Testing: Failure path names only `test_cache_invalidated_on_file_deletion`.
findings.finding: The new cache-HIT oracle in test_cache_miss_on_same_size_inplace_rewrite (inode unchanged) is never shown to detect a rewrite. The Testing section's failure path covers only the deletion test. Under the coarse-mtime fixture the old HIT oracle passes vacuously rather than failing. So the claim that the old oracle 'fails deterministically there' is false for this test, and the new oracle's ability to catch regressions is unproven.
scenarios: A regression makes the warm in-place path rewrite the cache. Under the fixture the mtime check passed anyway. The plan never demonstrates that the inode check fails in this case, so a mis-written inode oracle (e.g. stat taken after the call) would ship green.
findings.suggested_fix: In Testing, add: 'Failure path (HIT oracle): with the fixture active, temporarily force a rewrite before the HIT check (e.g. call atomic_write on the cache path), confirm `st_ino == before_ino` fails and `st_mtime_ns == before` still passes; record on the ticket.' Reword the Approach so only the deletion test's old oracle is said to fail under the fixture.

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Split AC1 into (a) a `[non-codebase]` attestation linking the recorded red output (old oracle failing under the fixture) on the ticket, and (b) a durable check with the exact command, e.g. `for i in $(seq 20); do pytest -q tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py::test_cache_invalidated_on_file_deletion tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py::test_cache_miss_on_same_size_inplace_rewrite || exit 1; done`.
evidence: "The root cause is identified with a deterministic reproduction (... recorded on this ticket), and the test asserts cache recomputation ... Checked by both tests passing 20 of 20 runs"
"pytest --count is not installed, so a shell loop" — loop not specified
findings.finding: AC1 bundles two different things. One is a one-time process attestation: the root cause was identified and the reproduction was recorded on the ticket. The other is a durable code outcome: the oracles do not depend on timestamp granularity. Its only proving check is '20 of 20 runs with the fixture active', which proves the second part but not the first. That check is also deterministic by design, so 20 runs adds no evidence over one, and the exact loop command is never written down.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — first checkbox; Testing — Happy path
scenarios: An executor runs the 20/20 loop and ticks AC1 without ever recording the red reproduction

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the '20 of 20 runs' gate with the deterministic pair it stands in for: under the coarse-mtime fixture, the old mtime oracle fails, and the new inode/envelope oracles pass, with the 20-run loop at most an optional extra check on the real coarse-timestamp host.
evidence: Plan: 'Every run then executes both tests under the conditions of the failing host. The old mtime oracle fails deterministically there'
Plan: 'with the new oracles, both tests pass under the fixture, 20 of 20 runs (`pytest --count` is not installed, so a shell loop)'
src/rebar/reducer/_cache.py:116-117: the envelope `{dir_hash, state}` is written via `atomic_write`, so the inode and envelope oracles are pure functions of the write sequence, not of clock timing
findings.finding: The acceptance criterion and the Testing section require '20 of 20 runs' as the stability evidence. But the coarse-mtime fixture makes the condition deterministic: every rewrite keeps the earlier mtime. The inode, dir_hash and envelope oracles do not depend on timing either. Repeating a deterministic test 20 times adds no signal. That is a ritual copied from flaky-test practice, where the real flake was probabilistic (16/30, 18/30), and it does not fit the deterministic design this plan builds.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, first bullet ('Checked by both tests passing 20 of 20 runs with the coarse-mtime fixture active') and Testing > Happy path
scenarios: A reviewer reads '20 of 20' as the real evidence and skips the more meaningful check: the old mtime oracle fails under the fixture 1 of 1, and the new oracles pass 1 of 1.
The shell-loop ritual gets copied into later deterministic-fixture fixes as if it were needed.
findings.suggested_fix: Change AC1's check to: 'Under the module-local coarse-mtime fixture, the old mtime assertion fails (recorded on the ticket) and both tests pass with the new inode + envelope oracles; optionally, 20/20 on the colima/overlayfs host as field confirmation.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the coarse-mtime fixture record each atomic_write call targeting .cache.json. The hit check asserts zero writes during the hit step, and the deletion test asserts exactly one write, alongside or instead of (st_dev, st_ino) comparison.
evidence: "every rewrite gives .cache.json a new inode, and an untouched cache keeps its inode"
"It wraps rebar.reducer._cache.atomic_write with monkeypatch" — the wrapper can record calls
"the only cache write seam, src/rebar/reducer/_cache.py:117"
findings.finding: The cache-hit oracle 'inode is unchanged' has two blind spots. First, inode numbers can be reused: if the hit step rewrites twice, the second temp file can take the original inode freed by the first replace, on ext4-backed /tmp such as GitHub runners. Second, it relies on atomic_write always using mkstemp+replace, so a future in-place write would pass the hit check silently. The plan's own fixture already wraps the only write seam, so it could count cache writes directly. A count does not depend on inode or timestamp behaviour.
findings.location: Approach — 'In-place-rewrite test: the cache-hit check asserts the inode is unchanged'
scenarios: A regression rewrites the cache twice on a hit, inode numbers are reused, and st_ino matches
A refactor of fsutil.atomic_write to write in place makes the hit check pass even on a rewrite
findings.suggested_fix: Have the fixture yield a list of written paths. In the in-place test assert `writes_during_hit == []`; in the deletion test assert exactly one post-deletion write to the cache path, plus the dir_hash and state checks. Keep the inode check only as a secondary assertion, comparing the (st_dev, st_ino) tuple.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC that the reducer-processors mutation shard's clean baseline passes with the change, or state explicitly that `make verify` runs that baseline.
evidence: "It is in the reducer-processors mutation shard, so a failure there fails that shard's clean baseline."
ACs: only the 20/20 loop and "make verify exits 0"
findings.finding: The Observation names the impact: the test sits in the reducer-processors mutation shard, and its flakiness fails that shard's clean baseline. No acceptance criterion or test step checks that shard's baseline after the change. `make verify` is the only repo-wide check, and the plan never says it runs the mutation shard. The new fixture's monkeypatch of atomic_write is also exactly the kind of change that can interact with mutation runs.
scenarios: make verify passes, but the mutation shard's baseline still fails or behaves differently under the monkeypatched seam

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the exact envelope assertion for the deletion test (the JSON key path to the comments list and the expected length 0) as a stated default.
evidence: "assert the inode changed, the envelope's dir_hash changed, and the cached state holds 0 comments"
"The cache envelope's dir_hash and state fields (_cache.py:116)"
findings.finding: The deletion oracle 'the cached state holds 0 comments' does not name the envelope path or the comparison. For example, it could be `envelope['state']['comments'] == []` or a len() check. The executor has to read _cache.py to work out the shape of `state`.
scenarios: The executor asserts against the wrong key and gets a KeyError, or a check that is always true

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Strengthen the in-place-rewrite HIT oracle beyond inode equality, e.g. assert that the atomic_write wrapper recorded zero writes to the cache path during the warm call, or pair the inode check with an unchanged envelope comparison.
evidence: "In-place-rewrite test: the cache-hit check asserts the inode is unchanged."
The deletion test pairs the inode check with dir_hash and state checks; the HIT test gets no equivalent.
findings.finding: Proving a cache HIT with inode equality alone is open to inode reuse. If a regression causes two rewrites between the 'before' stat and the check, the second temp file can reuse the freed original inode (common on ext4/tmpfs), and the HIT assertion passes falsely. Unlike the deletion test, the HIT test has no second, content-based signal.
findings.location: Approach: 'In-place-rewrite test: the cache-hit check asserts the inode is unchanged.'
scenarios: A regression writes the cache twice on a warm call. Inode A is freed after the first replace and reused by the second mkstemp. st_ino matches and the test reports a HIT that never happened.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the module-local fixture record each atomic_write target path. In the HIT check, assert that no write to `.cache.json` happened during the warm call, alongside the inode-unchanged check.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an end-state check that re-runs both tests 30x on the original overlayfs container, both with no sandbox and under bwrap, after the change, and records 0 failures on the ticket.
evidence: "Checked by both tests passing 20 of 20 runs with the coarse-mtime fixture active."
"In an ubuntu:26.04 container on a colima VM (Linux 6.8.0-117-generic, aarch64, overlayfs /tmp) ... failed 16 of 30 runs with no sandbox and 18 of 30 under bwrap."
findings.finding: Acceptance is checked only under the simulated coarse-mtime fixture on whatever host runs the suite. The plan never re-runs the original 30-run reproduction there after the change.

scenarios: overlayfs inode numbering behaves unexpectedly for upper-layer files on the original host. The fixture-based check passes on a dev machine, but the flake (or a new inode-based failure) persists on the host that reported it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to Testing/AC: 'On the ubuntu:26.04 colima container (overlayfs /tmp), run both tests 30 times with no sandbox and 30 times under bwrap after the change; 0 failures, recorded on the ticket.'
